items.statement: For every finite-dimensional real Hilbert/Borel space E, including rank zero, and signed real C2 compactly supported f, let gamma be the actual canonical stdGaussian E. The theorem internally produces true L1 of f squared, f squared times log(f squared), and the Hilbert norm of the true gradient squared, then proves homogeneous Ent_gamma(f squared)<=2 integral norm(gradient f)^2. Canonical basis law transport and orthonormal Parseval are internal; zero mass is included.
assumptions: E is any finite-dimensional complete real inner product space, with compatible norm and Borel measurable structure, including rank0. The basis is chosen internally; no positive-dimension assumption.

Only f, globally real C2 regularity and compact support are analytic premises. Signed functions/zero mass are included; no law, covariance, positivity, normalized mass, domain, gradient-Parseval or desired-inequality certificate is supplied.

gamma is literally Mathlib ProbabilityTheory.stdGaussian E. The actual canonical orthonormal basis sum of independent centered variance-one coordinates is identified with the continuous linear homeomorphism internally.

gradient is the literal global Mathlib Riesz Frechet representative. True coordinate chain rule and Parseval give its Hilbert norm squared; no default-Pi supremum operator norm or dimensional multiplier.
All3 L1 domains are conclusions. Measurable law transport and real map integrals carry true product-domain square, continuous tlogt and full energy from actual40.

Exact function-LSI coefficient2. Actual32 standardized RGO square-root-density cutoff test is a genuine consumer; cutoff exhaustion/coherent33 KL/Fisher, full noncompact/W12 LSI, separate GaussianT2/FIRST4.6 and both paper main/error/work/cost remain open.

formulae.label: Compact finite-Hilbert standard Gaussian log-Sobolev inequality
formulae.tex: \gamma=\mathrm{stdGaussian}(E),\qquad f\in C_c^2(E;\mathbb R),\qquad \operatorname{Ent}_{\gamma}(f^2)=\int f^2\log(f^2)\,d\gamma-\left(\int f^2\,d\gamma\right)\log\left(\int f^2\,d\gamma\right)\le2\int\|\nabla f\|^2\,d\gamma.
